nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the romance of the occult and the bestseller of the 1890s
literary_identity: Novelist; the most popular woman writer in England in the 1890s and the great populariser of the occult romance.
biography: Born Mary Mackay in London on 1 May 1855, the illegitimate daughter of the journalist Charles Mackay; she trained as a musician and took the name Marie Corelli, publishing A Romance of Two Worlds in 1886. The Sorrows of Satan (1895), The Mighty Atom (1896), The Murder of Delicia (1896) and The Master-Christian (1900) followed. She lived at Stratford-upon-Avon from 1899, where she campaigned for the Shakespeare memorial, and died there on 21 April 1924.
literary_profile: Corelli was the best-selling novelist in England in the 1890s and the first woman writer to outsell her male contemporaries by an enormous margin, with The Sorrows of Satan breaking every record of the trade. She gave the popular novel its taste for the occult, the oriental and the sensational, and her attacks on the literary establishment made her the first celebrity author in the modern sense.
stylistic_characteristics: The occult machinery of the romance — electricity, reincarnation, the astral body; the direct address to the reader and the authorial lecture; the sensational contrast of luxury and poverty; the florid, exclamatory, moralising prose; the melodramatic set-piece of the temptation.
intellectual_concerns: The reality of the soul and the survival of personality; the corruption of wealth and the metropolis; the hypocrisy of the churches; the position of the woman artist; the moral responsibility of fiction.
historical_significance: Marie Corelli was the most popular woman writer in England in the 1890s and the great populariser of the occult romance: The Sorrows of Satan broke the sales records of the trade, and her mixture of spiritualism, social protest and melodrama created the mass-market fiction of the twentieth century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British-American; the children's classic and the sentimental novel
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the author of Little Lord Fauntleroy, A Little Princess and The Secret Garden, and one of the most successful transatlantic writers of the period.
biography: Born Frances Eliza Hodgson in Manchester on 24 November 1849; her father died in 1853 and the family emigrated to Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1865. That Lass o' Lowrie's (1877) and Haworth's (1879) made her name, and Little Lord Fauntleroy (1886) made her rich. A Little Princess (1905) and The Secret Garden (1911) followed. She lived between England and America, married twice, and died at Plandome, New York, on 29 October 1924.
literary_profile: Burnett wrote three of the permanent children's classics in English and was one of the first writers to make a fortune from both the book and the dramatisation. Her transatlantic career, her business acumen and her invention of the children's novel of inner life gave the genre The Secret Garden, which remains the most widely read children's book of the period after Alice.
stylistic_characteristics: The child's-eye view of adult failure; the garden as a place of renewal; the orphan who remakes the household; the fairy-tale structure of loss and restoration; the plain, warm, direct prose of the story-teller.
intellectual_concerns: Childhood, illness and the recovery of the body; class and the servant problem as seen by a child; the healing power of place and cultivation; the orphan and the found family; the transatlantic crossing of manners.
historical_significance: Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote three permanent children's classics and was one of the first authors to make a fortune from both the book and the stage play: Little Lord Fauntleroy created the modern children's bestseller, and The Secret Garden became the most widely read children's book of the period after Alice in Wonderland.

literary_identity: Novelist and fruit farmer; the author of Lorna Doone, the most popular historical romance of the Victorian age after Scott.
biography: Born at Longworth, Berkshire, on 9 June 1825 and raised in Devon; he was educated at Blundell's and Exeter College, Oxford, trained as a barrister, and gave up the law for market gardening in Teddington. Lorna Doone appeared in 1869 and made him famous; The Maid of Sker (1872), Alice Lorraine (1875), Cripps the Carrier (1876) and Springhaven (1887) followed. He died at Teddington on 20 January 1900.
literary_profile: Blackmore wrote the most popular West Country romance in English and one of the great historical novels of the century: Lorna Doone has never been out of print, and its Exmoor landscape, its dialect and its narrative voice created the regional historical romance that Hardy and the West Country writers inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person Exmoor narrative in dialect-inflected prose; the slow accumulation of landscape and weather; the historical plot set in the seventeenth century; the love story interrupted by violence; the comic minor characters of the farm and the moor.
intellectual_concerns: The land and the labour of the farm; the border between England and the Celtic west; religious and political conflict in the seventeenth century; the rape and rescue of the heroine; the honest man against the great house.
historical_significance: R. D. Blackmore wrote the most popular West Country romance in English: Lorna Doone has never been out of print since 1869, and its Exmoor landscape and dialect narrative created the regional historical novel that Hardy inherited.

literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the most popular Scottish novelist of the 1870s and 1880s, and the inventor of the holiday romance of the Highlands and the sea.
biography: Born in Glasgow on 9 November 1841, the son of a manufacturer; he trained as a painter, turned to journalism, and made his name with A Daughter of Heth (1871). The Strange Adventures of a Phaeton (1872), The Princess of Thule (1873), Macleod of Dare (1878) and White Wings (1880) followed. He travelled constantly and died at Brighton on 10 December 1898.
literary_profile: Black wrote the most popular Scottish landscape romances of the 1870s and 1880s and invented the holiday novel in which the scenery of the Highlands and the Hebrides is itself the subject. His picture of the yacht, the hotel and the shooting lodge gave the Victorian reader the touring romance that Stevenson refined and that the twentieth-century Scottish novel inherited.
stylistic_characteristics: The touring narrative — coach, yacht, walking tour; the set-piece description of loch and mountain; the contrast of English visitor and Highland community; the light comedy of manners; the sentimental heroine of the islands.
intellectual_concerns: The Highlands and the clearances; the relation of the visitor to the native community; the place of women in a landscape romance; the commercialisation of scenery; the Celtic periphery and the English centre.
historical_significance: William Black was the most popular Scottish novelist of the 1870s and 1880s: his Highland and Hebridean romances invented the touring novel, made the scenery of the west of Scotland a literary property, and prepared the ground for the Scottish Renaissance.

literary_identity: Novelist and minister; the most prolific of the kailyard writers and the author of The Stickit Minister.
biography: Born at Duchrae, Balmaghie, in Galloway on 24 September 1859; he studied at Edinburgh University and the Free Church divinity hall, was ordained in 1886, and gave up the ministry for writing after The Stickit Minister (1893) became a bestseller. The Raiders (1894), The Lilac Sunbonnet (1894), Men of the Moss-Hags (1895) and a long series of Galloway romances followed. He died at Tarascon, France, on 16 April 1914.
literary_profile: Crockett was the most prolific of the kailyard writers and the one who gave the movement its historical dimension: his Galloway romances of the Covenanters, the gypsies and the smuggling trade carried the Scottish vernacular novel into the bestseller lists and made the south-west of Scotland a literary country.
stylistic_characteristics: The Galloway dialect in direct speech; the historical adventure of the Covenanting wars; the comic and pathetic minor characters; the rapid serial plot; the landscape of the Solway shore and the moor.
intellectual_concerns: Scottish national identity and the Covenanting past; the rural community and its oral culture; the relation of the minister to his people; poverty and the pride of the small farmer; emigration and the empty glen.
historical_significance: S. R. Crockett was the most prolific of the kailyard novelists and gave the movement its historical dimension: his Galloway romances of the Covenanters and the smugglers made the south-west of Scotland a literary country and carried the Scottish vernacular novel into the bestseller lists.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the kailyard ministry and the sentimental sketch
literary_identity: Minister and novelist; the pseudonym of John Watson, whose Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s.
biography: Born John Watson at Manningtree, Essex, on 3 November 1850 to Scottish parents; he was raised in Perthshire, studied at Edinburgh, and was minister of the Free Church at Logiealmond and then of Sefton Park Presbyterian Church, Liverpool. Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush (1894) sold in vast numbers; The Days of Auld Lang Syne (1895) and Kate Carnegie (1896) followed. He died at Mount Pleasant, Iowa, on 6 May 1907 while on a lecture tour.
literary_profile: Maclaren's Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s and the central text of the kailyard school: its sketches of the minister, the schoolmaster and the dying child created a sentimental image of the Scottish parish that dominated the popular imagination and provoked the reaction of George Douglas Brown and the Scottish Renaissance.
stylistic_characteristics: The linked sketch rather than the plotted novel; the dialect of the parish in direct speech; the deathbed scene and the consoling anecdote; the minister as narrator and moral centre; the short, sententious paragraph.
intellectual_concerns: The Presbyterian parish and its discipline; death, consolation and the life to come; poverty and the pride of the Scottish poor; education as the ladder out of the parish; the rural community against the modern city.
historical_significance: Ian Maclaren's Beside the Bonnie Brier Bush was the most popular Scottish book of the 1890s and the central text of the kailyard school: its sentimental parish sketches shaped the popular image of Scotland for a generation and provoked the realist reaction of The House with the Green Shutters.

literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of The House with the Green Shutters, the novel that destroyed the kailyard.
biography: Born George Douglas Brown at Ochiltree, Ayrshire, on 26 January 1869, the illegitimate son of a farmer; he studied at Glasgow and Oxford, worked as a journalist in London, and published The House with the Green Shutters under the name George Douglas in 1901. He died of pneumonia in London on 28 August 1902, at thirty-three.
literary_profile: The House with the Green Shutters is the single most important Scottish novel of the period and the book that ended the kailyard: its unsparing portrait of a small-town tyrant, its refusal of sentiment and its tragic ending gave Scottish fiction its first modern novel and made it the founding text of the Scottish Renaissance.
stylistic_characteristics: The objective, unsentimental narrative; the free indirect style that enters every mind in the town; the tragic structure of rise and fall; the grotesque and the violent detail; the Ayrshire vernacular in direct speech.
intellectual_concerns: The small town and its gossip; the tyranny of the father and the failure of the son; commercial ambition and bankruptcy; the provincial mind and the desire to escape; the death of the old Scotland.
historical_significance: The House with the Green Shutters is the most important Scottish novel of the period and the book that ended the kailyard school: its unsparing realism founded the modern Scottish novel and made it the direct ancestor of Lewis Grassic Gibbon and the Scottish Renaissance.

literary_identity: Methodist minister and novelist; the author of Her Benny, one of the most popular religious novels of the Victorian age.
biography: Born Silas Kitto Hocking at St Stephen-in-Brannel, Cornwall, on 24 March 1850; he was a Methodist minister in Liverpool and Manchester, and Her Benny (1879), the story of two Liverpool waifs, sold hundreds of thousands of copies. Alec Green (1881), Dick's Fairy (1883), The Strange Adventures of Israel Pendray (1899) and a long series of temperance and religious novels followed. He died at Southport on 16 September 1935.
literary_profile: Hocking wrote the most widely read Methodist popular novels of the Victorian age and Her Benny was one of the great bestsellers of the religious press, selling in the hundreds of thousands on both sides of the Atlantic. His temperance and waif narratives carried the evangelical novel into the mass market and gave the Victorian reader the sentimental street arab that Dickens had made respectable.
stylistic_characteristics: The waif narrative of the street and the workhouse; the deathbed scene of the pious child; the temperance plot of the drunkard's progress; the direct appeal to the reader's sympathy; the plain, emphatic, hortatory prose.
intellectual_concerns: Poverty and the street child; drink and the temperance cause; the Christian conversion and the good death; the city slum and the rural emigrant; the reward of virtue in this world and the next.
historical_significance: Silas Hocking wrote the most widely read Methodist popular novels of the Victorian age: Her Benny sold in the hundreds of thousands, carried the evangelical novel into the mass market, and gave the temperance movement its most effective piece of fiction.
